data.title: Company Valuation
data.statement:
You are helping a business owner estimate a company's value from its past annual profits.

For each of k consecutive years, you know the company's profit before tax (grossIncome) and its taxes. These statements are ordered from oldest to newest. Gross income here means profit after operating costs, including salaries, but before taxes. It does not mean revenue.

Calculate each historical net income as grossIncome - taxes. Fit a straight line to ALL historical net incomes using ordinary least squares with a free intercept. Use this line to forecast n years, then estimate the company's value by capitalizing the average forecast income.

The current year is the first year without a statement. It is also the FIRST of the n forecast years. Do not count it twice.

Assign x = 1 to the oldest statement and x = k to the latest statement. Let y be the corresponding historical net income. Calculate:

xMean = (k + 1) / 2
yMean = sum(y) / k
m = sum((x - xMean) * (y - yMean)) / sum((x - xMean)^2)
q = yMean - m * xMean
forecast(x) = m * x + q

Each sum covers all k historical statements. Using only the first and last statements is incorrect.

Forecast x = k + 1, k + 2, ..., k + n. The first forecast is the current-year income. Calculate the arithmetic mean of these n forecasts, then:

companyValue = averageProjectedIncome / capitalizationRate

The capitalization rate is supplied as a decimal: 0.10 means 10%. It affects companyValue only; it must not change the forecasts or their average.

Do not round intermediate calculations. Format the final output as described below. Negative forecasts and negative company values are valid results of this simplified model: do not replace them with zero. All input is valid; no error handling or exception output is required.

Example: historical net incomes 100000, 150000, 120000, 180000, 200000 give m = 23000 and q = 81000. With n = 3, the forecasts are 219000, 242000, 265000. Their average is 242000. With capitalizationRate = 0.10, companyValue = 2420000.

This is an educational model, not a guarantee of a company's actual sale price. The selected capitalization rate is an assumption, and a linear trend may produce economically unrealistic forecasts.

testCases.title: Linear growth with one forecast year
Linear growth with one forecast year - validator
Irregular income over five years - validator
Longer history and forecast horizon - validator
Declining income and final rounding - validator

data.constraints:
5 <= k <= 20
1 <= n <= 20
0 <= taxes <= grossIncome <= 1000000
grossIncome and taxes are integers.
0.0001 <= capitalizationRate <= 1
capitalizationRate uses ordinary decimal notation with at most four digits after the decimal point.
All input respects these constraints. Forecast incomes, their average, and the company value may be negative.

STATEMENT
Use every historical statement to forecast net income and estimate a company's value.

INPUT
k: Number of historical statements, ordered from oldest to newest.
n: Number of forecast years, including the current year.
capitalizationRate: Decimal capitalization rate; 0.10 means 10 percent.
grossIncome: Company profit before tax, after operating costs.
taxes: Company taxes for this historical year.

OUTPUT
Print historical net incomes, current-year income, forecast incomes, their average, and company value on five lines, with two decimal places.
data.inputDescription:
Line 1: two integers k and n, followed by a decimal capitalizationRate, separated by single spaces.

Next k lines: two integers grossIncome and taxes, separated by a single space, for one historical annual statement. Statements are ordered from oldest to newest.

k is the number of historical statements. n is the number of forecast years, including the current year. All monetary inputs use the same currency unit.
data.outputDescription:
Print exactly five lines, without labels:

Line 1: k historical net incomes, from oldest to newest, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the current-year income, which is the first forecast.
Line 3: n forecast incomes, starting with the current year, separated by single spaces.
Line 4: the arithmetic mean of the n forecast incomes.
Line 5: the company value, equal to the unrounded average forecast income divided by capitalizationRate.

Print every monetary value with exactly two digits after the decimal point. Use a dot as the decimal separator, without currency symbols or thousands separators.

Round each final value independently to the nearest hundredth. If a value is exactly halfway between two hundredths, round away from zero: 3.125 becomes 3.13 and -3.125 becomes -3.13. Print zero as 0.00, never -0.00. Do not round intermediate calculations or use a rounded average to calculate the company value.
